reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because the speaker promotes ETHConnect lending with a claim of up to 52% profit per month and directs viewers to sign up, deposit Ethereum, and lend it. The promotion also presents team-building as profitable and asks viewers to join the speaker's team through a signup link. The material describes the offer and solicitation, while not establishing that anyone deposited funds, received returns, or suffered a loss, or independently verifying the platform's claims.

citations.quote: fifty two percent in profit per month
you can lend
you can build yourself a team of investors
how much you can make off of each level

opening.argument: Judge the speaker's degree of certainty. He attributes the monthly return to what the platform says, rather than claiming to have verified a payout, and presents a comparison as a prediction rather than an established result. He also describes a future app with tentative language. Those qualifications matter: the video contains enthusiastic investment commentary, but these statements do not certify that the projected returns or features will materialize. The evidence supports a reading of speculative commentary about an emerging offer, not a claim that the speaker has confirmed its performance.

citations.quote: they're saying you can get up to fifty two percent in profit per month
some predict that is going to be greater than Bit Connect
Looks like they're gonna have an app here real soon in the next couple months.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The cited percentage is introduced as something “they're saying,” not as a return the speaker says he received. The opening also concedes that the material does not establish a deposit, payout, or loss. A quoted offer and an invitation to consider it can be evaluated critically without treating the projected rate as a verified outcome.

citations.quote: they're saying you can get up to fifty two percent in profit per month

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Attribution does not turn this into a warning or detached market analysis. The speaker follows the return claim with an immediate invitation to participate, and later tells viewers they can deposit and lend Ethereum that day. Tentative language about an app does not qualify the present call to put funds into the lending offer.

citations.quote: now is your opportunity to do so ETH Connect
But you can sign up today and start depositing. And start lending out Ethereum today

opening.argument: Much of what the viewer receives is a walkthrough of the project's own pages. The speaker identifies the ICO and lending information as material visible on screen, pauses to inspect a breakdown, and says he will zoom in. The sampled pages include a project description and navigation to a whitepaper. That supports reading the presentation as an explanation of what the site displays, rather than firsthand proof that its lending figures work. A judge should distinguish demonstrating a project's stated features from establishing the truth of every figure shown during the demonstration.

citations.quote: you see here on the screen the ICO has already started lending is available now
Here's kind of a breakdown of the setup there and how much you can make off of each level
Well, let me zoom in here.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference points to the rate and team-level figures, but those are precisely the kinds of claims a site walkthrough can display without validating them. The speaker's “here on the screen” framing and his pause to zoom in identify material being examined. The cited figures establish what the presentation shows, not whether the advertised returns were paid.

citations.quote: you see here on the screen
Well, let me zoom in here.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The walkthrough is part of the pitch. The speaker does not stop at describing the site: he says viewers can sign up and deposit now, then asks them to use his link and join his team. No proof of an actual payout is needed to recognize that he is promoting participation in the advertised lending and recruitment offer.

citations.quote: But you can sign up today and start depositing.
click on the link to sign up join my team

opening.argument: The visible mechanism could be read as a referral promotion for a service: the description supplies a referral link, while the speaker asks viewers to subscribe and join his team. Recruitment language alone does not show that anyone earned a commission, that a particular viewer transferred funds, or that a promised payment failed. Even the large monthly figure is phrased as an upper bound attributed to the platform, not a guaranteed personal payout. The record certainly warrants skepticism, but the observed link and invitation do not by themselves establish what happened after a viewer clicked.

citations.quote: Click the link below! Start your money machine! https://ethconnect.net/ref/redplanet32
click on the link to sign up join my team
they're saying you can get up to fifty two percent in profit per month

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference identifies a lending pitch and level-based earnings, but it also acknowledges that no completed deposit or payout is established. The quoted material is an invitation and a description of what participants might make, not evidence of an actual transaction or realized downline income. Those limits matter when deciding how much the presentation proves.

citations.quote: how much you can make off of each level
click on the link to sign up join my team

true_side_reply.rebuttal: This is not merely a generic referral discount. The speaker invites viewers to deposit and lend Ethereum while promoting a claimed monthly profit, then explicitly says they can profit from building an investor team. The concern is the offer being promoted; showing that a viewer completed a transfer is not required to identify that promotion.
